title: Traps and fishing
summary: Set many traps on active game trails, and leave several baited lines out overnight.

blocks.p: Outside a genuine emergency, trapping, snaring and set lines are regulated or illegal in most places. Check your state’s rules before practising.

list: Set traps on active game trails, at spots where the trail narrows, and near water, dens or feeding signs.
Set many. Most traps catch nothing, so a dozen beats one.
Handle them as little as possible and leave the trail undisturbed. Check them at least once a day.
Simple snare: a loop of wire or strong cord with a sliding noose, anchored firmly. For rabbits, make the loop about fist-sized with its bottom about 3 inches above the trail.

blocks.cap: Simple snare across a trail. Disturb the trail as little as possible.

list: Squirrel pole: lean a long pole against a tree squirrels use and fix several small snares along it.

blocks.cap: Squirrels take the easy route up a leaning pole.

list: Figure-4 deadfall: three notched sticks hold up a heavy rock or log, and bait on the trigger stick drops it. Keep your hands and body out from under the weight while setting it.

blocks.cap: Figure-4 deadfall. Disturbing the bait trips the trigger and drops the weight.

list: Gorge hook: a short sliver of bone or hardwood, sharpened at both ends and tied at the middle. Bait it; it lodges crosswise when swallowed.
Fish trap: a funnel of stakes in shallow water that fish swim into but struggle to find their way out of.
Several baited lines left out overnight catch more than one rod you have to watch.
Fish feed most around dawn and dusk.

blocks.cap: Gorge hook and a stake fish trap, seen from above.
